title: Carpet Shampoo vs Extraction Cleaning
excerpt: Carpet shampoo suspends soil with foaming chemistry and agitation; extraction cleaning uses liquid and suction to flush and recover suspended soil and moisture. Both require compatibility and complete drying.
content_html:
Carpet shampoo and extraction cleaning are both wet restorative methods, but they remove soil differently. Shampoo relies heavily on detergent foam and agitation. Extraction applies liquid and then uses suction to recover suspended soil and moisture from the carpet.

How carpet shampoo works

Rotary shampoo systems work cleaning chemistry into the pile with mechanical agitation. Industry guidance describes shampoo as a restorative method in which suspended soil and cleaning material are removed by wet vacuuming or subsequent removal steps, depending on the system.

How extraction works

Hot-water extraction applies water or cleaning solution to the carpet and immediately recovers liquid with vacuum suction. The process acts as a rinse-and-recovery system for suspended soil. EPA identifies periodic wet extraction as an important carpet-maintenance method in schools.

Residue control differs

Shampoo methods depend on correct detergent use and effective recovery because remaining cleaning material can contribute to film or resoiling. Extraction can also leave residue if the chemistry is overdosed or not adequately rinsed and recovered.

Mechanical action differs

Shampoo generally uses more direct agitation to distribute foam and loosen soil. Extraction systems may use a wand, self-contained machine or powered agitation, but the defining step is recovery of liquid and suspended soil by extraction.

Drying is critical for both

EPA and GSA both emphasise drying after wet carpet cleaning. GSA requires extraction-cleaned public-area carpet to be dry before customers occupy the building, and EPA warns that persistent carpet moisture can support mold growth.

Comparison

FeatureShampooExtraction
Main mechanismFoaming chemistry + agitationLiquid application + vacuum recovery
Soil removalSuspension followed by recovery/removalSuspension plus physical liquid extraction
Residue concernDetergent left after incomplete removalChemistry or soil left after inadequate rinse/recovery
Drying needMust dry completelyMust dry completely

Which method is right?

Choose from the carpet manufacturer's maintenance requirements, carpet construction, soil load, equipment capability and drying window. Neither label alone guarantees a good result; correct chemistry, agitation, recovery and drying determine performance.

Practical takeaway

Shampoo is primarily a foam-and-agitation system; extraction is primarily a rinse-and-recovery system. In both cases, control detergent, recover as much soil and moisture as the system allows and return the carpet to use only after it is dry.
